source.text: Παῦλος κλητὸς ἀπόστολος Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ διὰ θελήματος θεοῦ καὶ Σωσθένης ὁ ἀδελφὸς τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ τοῦ θεοῦ, ἡγιασμένοις ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, τῇ οὔσῃ ἐν Κορίνθῳ, κλητοῖς ἁγίοις, σὺν πᾶσιν τοῖς ἐπικαλουμένοις τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ αὐτῶν καὶ ἡμῶν·

records.literal_gloss: Paul, called apostle of Christ Jesus through [the] will of God, and Sosthenes the brother, \v 2 to the church of the God, having been made holy in Christ Jesus, the [one] being in Corinth, called holy [ones], with all the [ones] calling on the name of the Lord of us Jesus Christ in every place, of them and of us;

en.L: Paul, a called apostle of {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus through [the] will of God, and Sosthenes [our] brother, \v 2 to the church of God, [to those] made holy in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus, [the church] that is in Corinth, called holy ones, together with all who call on the name of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} in every place, theirs and ours.
en.B: From Paul, called by the will of God to be an apostle of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus, and from Sosthenes our brother, \v 2 to the church of God in Corinth: to you who have been made holy in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus, a holy people by God's call, together with all who call on the name of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} in every place, the Lord who is theirs as well as ours.
en.R: This letter is from Paul and from our brother Sosthenes. God called me, Paul, to be an apostle, sent out by {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus. It was God's will. \v 2 We are writing to God's church in the city of Corinth. God has made you holy because you belong to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus. He has called you to be {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} holy people, together with everyone, everywhere, who prays to our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}. He is their Lord as well as ours.

decisions.choice: called apostle: an apostle because God called him, a messenger sent out with the authority of the one who sends him
alternatives: an apostle by his own choice
an apostle appointed by a church
decisions.reason: κλητὸς ("called") stands before ἀπόστολος ("apostle"): Paul holds his office because God called him, and "through the will of God" says the same again (compare Galatians 1:1, 1:15). An apostle is one sent out to speak for the one who sends him, as in Colossians 1:1. The same word, κλητοῖς, describes the Corinthians in verse 2: Paul and the church owe their standing to the same call. In a letter to a church that was ranking its teachers (1:12; 9:1-3), Paul rests his authority on God's call, not on his own gifts.

decisions.choice: Sosthenes: a fellow believer known to the Corinthians, perhaps the synagogue leader named in Acts 18:17
decisions.reason: Acts 18:17 tells of a Sosthenes, leader of the synagogue in Corinth, who was beaten in front of the governor Gallio's court. If this is the same man, he had since come to faith and was now with Paul. The name was common, so the link is possible, not certain. "The brother" means a fellow believer.

decisions.choice: the church of God: the assembly of God's people in Corinth, a body of people, not a building, and one that belongs to God
decisions.reason: ἐκκλησίᾳ was the word for the gathered citizen assembly of a Greek city, and the Greek Old Testament uses it for the assembly of Israel gathered before God (Deuteronomy 4:10; 23:1-3). "Of God" says whose it is: not Paul's, Apollos's or Cephas's (1:12), but God's. The first churches met in homes (16:19).

decisions.choice: made holy and called holy: they already belong to God, set apart by him in Christ, and they are holy people because he called them
alternatives: called to become holy, as a goal still to be reached
decisions.reason: ἡγιασμένοις is a perfect participle: they have been made holy, and remain so (6:11). κλητοῖς ἁγίοις means "called holy ones": God's call makes them his holy people, as Israel was (Exodus 19:6; Philippians 1:1). This is what they are, not a prize to be won. It is all the more striking because the letter goes on to correct serious faults in this church. ἡγιασμένοις is masculine plural though "church" is feminine: Paul moves from the church to its people.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "made holy in Christ Jesus" before "that is in Corinth"
alternatives: "to the church of God that is in Corinth, made holy in Christ Jesus"
decisions.reason: Manuscripts differ in the order of these two phrases. The SBLGNT follows early manuscripts that put "made holy in Christ Jesus" first, which leaves "that is in Corinth" oddly separated from "church"; other manuscripts have the smoother order, which a copyist was more likely to create than to undo. The meaning is the same either way. Reviewers should check the apparatus.

decisions.choice: call on the name of the Lord: pray to and worship Jesus as Lord, in the words the Old Testament uses for calling on God
alternatives: simply bear the name of Jesus
decisions.reason: In the Old Testament people "call on the name" of God in prayer and worship (Genesis 4:26; Psalm 116:4), and Joel 2:32 promises that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved; there the Hebrew has God's own name. Paul quotes that verse of Jesus in Romans 10:13. Here the same act of worship is directed to "our Lord Jesus Christ". The Corinthians are reminded that they are one with believers everywhere who do the same.

decisions.choice: theirs and ours: Jesus is their Lord as well as ours
alternatives: in every place, theirs and ours: the places where they and we live
decisions.reason: αὐτῶν καὶ ἡμῶν ("of them and of us") could go with "our Lord" or with "every place". Taken with "Lord", it says that the one Lord belongs to all his people alike, a point the divided Corinthians needed (1:13). Taken with "place", it adds little to "in every place". The Literal keeps the Greek order and leaves the question open.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "called apostle of Christ Jesus"
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts reverse the two names, and a few leave out "called". The meaning does not change, so there is no footnote.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: holy ones (L); a holy people (B); God's holy people (R)
decisions.reason: As in Philippians 1:1: in current English "saints" suggests unusually good people or those honored by a church, while Paul is writing to the whole congregation.

decisions.choice: the Lord who is theirs as well as ours (B); He is their Lord as well as ours (R)
alternatives: in every place, theirs and ours
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable follow meaning decision m7; the Literal keeps the Greek order, which leaves the question open.

decisions.choice: prays to
decisions.reason: "Call on the name" is Bible language for prayer and worship (m6); Readable says it in everyday words.

decisions.choice: This letter is from Paul ... God called me, Paul, to be an apostle ... It was God's will.
alternatives: Paul, called to be an apostle ... through the will of God
decisions.reason: Readable turns the opening of the letter into ordinary sentences, as Philippians 1:1 and Colossians 1:1 do.

source.text: χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη ἀπὸ θεοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν καὶ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: Grace to you and peace from God Father of us and Lord Jesus Christ.

en.L: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and [the] Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.
en.B: Grace and peace to you from God our Father and from the Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.
en.R: I pray that God our Father and the Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} will show you grace and give you peace.

decisions.choice: one source: God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ together
decisions.reason: A single ἀπὸ ("from") governs both names, so Jesus is named with God the Father as the one source of grace and peace. Paul opens almost every letter this way (Romans 1:7; Philippians 1:2).

decisions.choice: a greeting turned into a blessing
decisions.reason: Greek letters normally opened with a one-word "greetings". Paul replaces it with χάρις (grace), a word close to it in sound, and adds εἰρήνη (peace), the usual Jewish greeting. It is a wish and a prayer for God's favor and wholeness.

decisions.choice: Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: I pray that ... will show you grace and give you peace
decisions.reason: The greeting has no verb. Readable states it as the prayer it is, as Philippians 1:2 does.

source.text: Εὐχαριστῶ τῷ θεῷ μου πάντοτε περὶ ὑμῶν ἐπὶ τῇ χάριτι τοῦ θεοῦ τῇ δοθείσῃ ὑμῖν ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, ὅτι ἐν παντὶ ἐπλουτίσθητε ἐν αὐτῷ, ἐν παντὶ λόγῳ καὶ πάσῃ γνώσει, καθὼς τὸ μαρτύριον τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐβεβαιώθη ἐν ὑμῖν, ὥστε ὑμᾶς μὴ ὑστερεῖσθαι ἐν μηδενὶ χαρίσματι, ἀπεκδεχομένους τὴν ἀποκάλυψιν τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ·

records.literal_gloss: I give thanks to the God of me always concerning you for the grace of the God the [one] having been given to you in Christ Jesus, \v 5 that in everything you were made rich in him, in all speech and all knowledge, \v 6 just as the testimony of the Christ was confirmed in you, \v 7 so that you not to be lacking in no gift, awaiting the revelation of the Lord of us Jesus Christ;

en.L: I thank my God always concerning you for the grace of God that was given to you in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus, \v 5 that in everything you were made rich in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, in all speech and all knowledge, \v 6 just as the testimony of the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} was confirmed in you, \v 7 so that you do not lack any gift, as you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.
en.B: I give thanks to my God for you at all times, because of the grace God gave you in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus. \v 5 In {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} you have been made rich in everything: in every kind of speaking and every kind of knowledge. \v 6 In this way the witness to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} was made firm among you, \v 7 and so you fall short in no gift of grace while you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.
en.R: I always thank my God for you, because of the grace {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has given you in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus. \v 5 Because you belong to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, God has made you rich in every way: in all you say and in all you know. \v 6 This shows that the message we told you about {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} has taken firm root in you. \v 7 So you have every gift that God in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} grace gives, while you wait for the day when our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} will appear.

decisions.choice: the grace given in Christ Jesus: God's free favor, given when they came to belong to Christ and seen in their gifts (verses 5-7)
decisions.reason: δοθείσῃ ("given") is an aorist and points back to a definite time, when the Corinthians believed. "In Christ Jesus" says where the gift is found: in union with him. Verses 5-7 then say what the grace has produced among them.

decisions.choice: speech and knowledge: gifts of speaking (teaching, prophecy, tongues) and of understanding God's ways
alternatives: eloquence and learning as human skills
decisions.reason: λόγῳ and γνώσει name things the Corinthians prized, and the letter comes back to both (8:1; 12:8; 13:1-2; 14:1-25). Paul thanks God for them as gifts before he corrects the way the church uses them.

decisions.choice: the testimony about Christ, made firm among them
alternatives: the testimony that Christ himself gave
decisions.reason: Χριστοῦ names whom the testimony is about: the message Paul bore witness to when he came to Corinth (2:1-2; 15:15). ἐβεβαιώθη means confirmed or made firm, a word also used for a legal guarantee (compare Philippians 1:7). The gifts the church received showed that the message had taken hold.

decisions.choice: gift: a particular gift of God's grace
alternatives: only the miraculous gifts of the Spirit
decisions.reason: χαρίσματι is built from the word for grace and means something given freely. Paul uses it for any gift of grace (Romans 6:23; 1 Corinthians 7:7), including the gifts of the Spirit discussed in chapters 12-14. The link with the grace of verse 4 is deliberate.

decisions.choice: the revealing of the Lord: his coming in glory at the end, for which they eagerly wait
decisions.reason: ἀποκάλυψιν is an unveiling. Paul uses it of the Lord Jesus being revealed from heaven (2 Thessalonians 1:7), and verse 8 speaks of "the day of our Lord". ἀπεκδεχομένους is a strong word for eager waiting (Philippians 3:20). The gifts belong to this time of waiting, not to the end itself (13:8-12).

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "my God"
decisions.reason: A few important early manuscripts do not have "my". It is easy to see a copyist either adding it from Philippians 1:3 or dropping it. The meaning is not changed.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting. Literal keeps the article in verse 6: "the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}".

decisions.choice: gift of grace (B); every gift that God in his grace gives (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable keep the link with "grace" in verse 4 that the Greek word carries (m4).

decisions.choice: Because you belong to him; This shows that the message we told you about Christ has taken firm root in you; the day when our Lord Jesus Christ will appear
alternatives: just as the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you
the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ
decisions.reason: Readable says what "in him" means, how the gifts show that the message took hold (m3), and what the "revealing" of the Lord is (m5).

source.text: ὃς καὶ βεβαιώσει ὑμᾶς ἕως τέλους ἀνεγκλήτους ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: who also will confirm you until [the] end blameless in the day of the Lord of us Jesus Christ.

en.L: [He] who will also confirm you to [the] end, blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.
en.B: He will also keep you firm to the end, so that you will be free from any charge on the day of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.
en.R: He will keep you strong to the very end, so that no one will be able to accuse you of anything on the day our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} comes back.

decisions.choice: who: most likely God, who gave the grace (verse 4) and whose faithfulness verse 9 names; the words may also point to Jesus Christ, named just before
decisions.reason: The relative pronoun ὃς most naturally refers to the last person named, Jesus Christ at the end of verse 7. But the sentence goes on to "the day of our Lord Jesus Christ", which reads oddly if Christ is the subject, and verse 9 gives the ground of this promise: "God is faithful." Every level keeps the subject unnamed ("who", "He"), as the Greek does.

decisions.choice: confirm, keep firm: God will hold them steady and secure
decisions.reason: βεβαιώσει is the verb of verse 6 again: as the message about Christ was made firm among them, so they themselves will be made firm. The word was also used of a legal guarantee.

decisions.choice: blameless: with no charge that can be brought against them
decisions.reason: ἀνεγκλήτους is a word from the law court: no accusation will stand (compare Colossians 1:22). Paul pictures the coming day as a judgment at which they will be found clear.

decisions.choice: the day of our Lord: the Old Testament day of God's judgment, now the day of Jesus' coming
decisions.reason: The prophets spoke of "the day of the Lord", when God would come to judge and to save (Amos 5:18; Joel 2:31). Paul gives the day to Jesus (5:5; Philippians 1:6), connecting it with his "revealing" in verse 7.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "our Lord Jesus Christ"
decisions.reason: A few early manuscripts end the verse with "Jesus" and do not have "Christ". The meaning does not change. Reviewers should check the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: [He] who (L); He (B, R)
decisions.reason: Each level leaves the subject unnamed, so as not to decide what the Greek leaves open (m1). A sentence beginning with a bare "who" is not possible in English, so Literal supplies "[He]".

decisions.choice: free from any charge (B); no one will be able to accuse you of anything (R)
decisions.reason: "Blameless" can sound like a claim of perfect behavior. Balanced and Readable keep the law-court sense (m3), as Colossians 1:22 does.

source.text: πιστὸς ὁ θεὸς δι’ οὗ ἐκλήθητε εἰς κοινωνίαν τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν.

records.literal_gloss: Faithful [is] the God, through whom you were called into fellowship of the Son of him, Jesus Christ the Lord of us.

en.L: God [is] faithful, through whom you were called into [the] fellowship of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Son, Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} our Lord.
en.B: God is faithful. It was {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} who called you to share in the life of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Son, Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} our Lord.
en.R: You can depend on God. He is the one who called you to be joined to {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Son, Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} our Lord, and to share {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} life.

decisions.choice: faithful: God can be relied on to keep his word and finish what he began
decisions.reason: πιστὸς here means trustworthy. The promise of verse 8 rests on God's faithfulness, as it does in 10:13 and 1 Thessalonians 5:24. It stands first in the sentence for emphasis.

decisions.choice: through whom you were called: God himself is the one who called them
alternatives: God called them through someone else
decisions.reason: "Through" usually names a go-between, but here οὗ ("whom") is God himself, as in Romans 11:36. The call is God's own act, the call that made them "called holy ones" (verse 2).

decisions.choice: fellowship of his Son: a shared life with the Son, and in him with one another
alternatives: partnership in a task (as in Philippians 1:5)
decisions.reason: κοινωνίαν means having a share in something together. With "of his Son" it means sharing in the Son himself: belonging to him and having a part in his life (compare 10:16, where the cup is a sharing in the blood of Christ). The word prepares for the appeal of verse 10: people who all share in one Son cannot be divided into parties.

decisions.choice: his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord: the opening names Jesus as Lord again and again
decisions.reason: In verses 1-10 Paul names "our Lord Jesus Christ" in nearly every sentence. Here the full title closes the thanksgiving: the one the Corinthians share is God's own Son and their Lord, not any human teacher.

decisions.choice: Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: share in the life of (B); be joined to ... and to share his life (R)
decisions.reason: "Fellowship" today often means a friendly gathering. Balanced and Readable say what it means here (m3).

decisions.choice: You can depend on God
decisions.reason: Readable says what "faithful" means here (m1).

source.text: Παρακαλῶ δὲ ὑμᾶς, ἀδελφοί, διὰ τοῦ ὀνόματος τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ἵνα τὸ αὐτὸ λέγητε πάντες, καὶ μὴ ᾖ ἐν ὑμῖν σχίσματα, ἦτε δὲ κατηρτισμένοι ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ νοῒ καὶ ἐν τῇ αὐτῇ γνώμῃ.

records.literal_gloss: I urge but you, brothers, through the name of the Lord of us Jesus Christ, that the same [thing] you say all, and not be among you divisions, you be but having been restored in the same mind and in the same judgment.

en.L: Now I urge you, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, by the name of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, that you all say the same thing, and [that] there be no divisions among you, but [that] you be restored in the same mind and in the same judgment.
en.B: Now, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, I urge you by the name of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}: agree with one another, all of you, and let there be no splits among you. Let what is torn be mended, so that you are joined together, one in mind and one in purpose.
en.R: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, I urge you in the name of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}: agree with each other. Do not split up into groups. Be united again, so that you share the same way of thinking and the same goals.

decisions.choice: I urge you by the name of our Lord: a strong appeal, made on the authority of Christ
alternatives: I beg you as a favor
decisions.reason: Παρακαλῶ can mean to comfort, but here it is a strong request. Paul makes it "by the name" of the Lord Jesus Christ: the appeal rests on Christ's authority, and it is the name into which they were baptized (verses 13 and 15), not the name of any teacher.

decisions.choice: say the same thing: be in agreement, with no rival parties
alternatives: hold identical opinions on every matter
decisions.reason: The phrase was used in Greek writing for parties that settle a quarrel and come to agreement. Paul is not asking for one opinion on every question; he wants an end to the rival slogans of verse 12.

decisions.choice: divisions: splits within the one church, not yet separate churches
decisions.reason: σχίσματα is a tear, as in a torn garment (Mark 2:21). The Corinthians still met together (11:18 uses the same word for divisions at their gatherings), but they were torn by rival loyalties.

decisions.choice: restored, mended: put back into good working order
decisions.reason: κατηρτισμένοι is used for mending nets (Mark 1:19) and for restoring a person who has fallen (Galatians 6:1). The picture answers the "tear" of the divisions. The perfect participle points to a settled state: mended and staying so.

decisions.choice: the same mind and the same judgment: one way of thinking and one settled purpose
decisions.reason: νοῒ is the mind, a person's way of thinking; γνώμῃ is an opinion or decision reached. Together they mean a shared outlook and a shared aim (compare Philippians 2:2).

decisions.choice: {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}
decisions.reason: Paul writes to the whole church, women and men; Chloe's people bring the report (verse 11), and the letter speaks to women directly (7:10-16; 11:5). "Brothers" stays available as the traditional form.

decisions.choice: Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: agree with one another (B); agree with each other (R)
decisions.reason: The idiom means being in agreement (m2); Literal keeps its form.

decisions.choice: Let what is torn be mended, so that you are joined together
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the picture of mending what is torn (m3, m4).

source.text: ἐδηλώθη γάρ μοι περὶ ὑμῶν, ἀδελφοί μου, ὑπὸ τῶν Χλόης ὅτι ἔριδες ἐν ὑμῖν εἰσιν.

records.literal_gloss: It was made clear for to me concerning you, brothers of me, by the [ones] of Chloe, that quarrels among you there are.

en.L: For it has been made clear to me about you, my {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, by those of Chloe, that there are quarrels among you.
en.B: I say this, my {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, because Chloe's people have made it clear to me that rivalries have broken out among you.
en.R: Some people from Chloe's household have told me about you, my {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}. They say that you are arguing with each other.

decisions.choice: Chloe's people: members of a household or business headed by a woman named Chloe
decisions.reason: τῶν Χλόης is "those of Chloe", with no noun. The phrase usually means members of someone's household: family, slaves or freed slaves, or agents traveling on business. Chloe is not mentioned anywhere else. She may have lived in Corinth or in Ephesus, where Paul was writing (16:8); the Corinthians clearly knew who she was. Women such as Lydia (Acts 16:14-15) headed households among the first believers.

decisions.choice: quarrels: rivalries and arguments
decisions.reason: ἔριδες is strife or rivalry, a word Paul lists among the works of the flesh (Galatians 5:20) and uses of the Corinthians again in 3:3. It names the wrangling behind the slogans of verse 12.

decisions.choice: made clear: a definite report from people Paul names, not rumor
decisions.reason: ἐδηλώθη means shown or made plain. Paul names his source openly, so the church knows the report is not gossip.

decisions.choice: my {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}
decisions.reason: As in verse 10: the letter is written to women and men.

decisions.choice: Chloe's people (B); some people from Chloe's household (R)
decisions.reason: The phrase has no noun (m1). Balanced keeps it open; Readable says what it usually meant.

decisions.choice: I say this ... because
decisions.reason: Balanced spells out how "for" links the report to the appeal of verse 10.

source.text: λέγω δὲ τοῦτο ὅτι ἕκαστος ὑμῶν λέγει· Ἐγὼ μέν εἰμι Παύλου, Ἐγὼ δὲ Ἀπολλῶ, Ἐγὼ δὲ Κηφᾶ, Ἐγὼ δὲ Χριστοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: I mean but this, that each of you says, I on the one hand am of Paul, I but of Apollos, I but of Cephas, I but of Christ.

en.L: Now I mean this, that each of you says, "I am of Paul," "But I of Apollos," "But I of Cephas," "But I of {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}."
en.B: What I mean is that every one of you takes a side: "I am for Paul," "I am for Apollos," "I am for Cephas," "I am for {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}."
en.R: Here is what I mean. Each of you is taking sides. One says, "I am on Paul's side." Another says, "I am on Apollos's side." Another says, "I am on Peter's side." And another says, "I am on {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}'s side."

decisions.choice: I am of Paul: I belong to Paul's party, I am his follower
alternatives: I am Paul's disciple in a formal school
decisions.reason: The genitive Παύλου ("of Paul") marks belonging: the speaker claims to be Paul's man. These are slogans, the cries of supporters. ἕκαστος ("each") suggests that the rivalry had drawn in the whole church.

decisions.choice: Apollos: a Jewish believer from Alexandria, a gifted speaker who taught in Corinth after Paul
decisions.reason: Acts 18:24-19:1 describes Apollos as learned and eloquent, and says he went to Corinth after Paul left. Paul treats him as a fellow worker, not a rival (3:4-9; 16:12).

decisions.choice: Cephas: Peter, called by his Aramaic name
decisions.reason: Κηφᾶ is the Greek form of an Aramaic word meaning "rock", the name Jesus gave Simon (John 1:42); Paul uses it for Peter (15:5; Galatians 2:9). Whether Peter had visited Corinth is not known; 9:5 says he traveled with his wife.

decisions.choice: "I am of Christ": a fourth slogan, claiming Christ for one group against the others
alternatives: Paul's own reply to the slogans: "but I belong to Christ"
decisions.reason: The words have the same form as the other three slogans, and verse 13 answers them with "Is Christ divided?" In 3:23 Paul says that all of them belong to Christ; the fault here is to make Christ the badge of one party. Some read the words as Paul's own answer, but nothing marks them off from the others.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: I am for Paul (B); I am on Paul's side (R)
decisions.reason: These are the cries of rival supporters (m1); Balanced and Readable use the language of taking sides.

decisions.choice: Peter
decisions.reason: Readable uses the name most readers know; Literal and Balanced keep Cephas, the name Paul uses (m3).

source.text: μεμέρισται ὁ Χριστός;

records.literal_gloss: Has been divided the Christ?

en.L: Has the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} been divided?
en.B: Has {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} been parceled out?
en.R: Can {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} be cut up, with a piece for each group?

decisions.choice: a question, as the SBLGNT prints it, expecting the answer "no"
alternatives: a statement: "Christ has been divided up!"
decisions.reason: The Greek has no question word, so μεμέρισται ὁ Χριστός could also be read as a bitter statement of what the slogans have done. Read as a question, it opens the series of three questions that follows.

decisions.choice: divided: split up and shared out in portions
decisions.reason: μεμέρισται means to divide into parts or to hand out shares. Each party behaves as if it owned its own portion of Christ. The perfect tense pictures the result: Christ cut up and parceled out.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: no negative particle at the start
alternatives: with μή: "Christ has not been divided, has he?"
decisions.reason: Some early manuscripts begin with the particle μή, which turns the words into a question expecting "no", like the next sentence. It is probably taken from there. The meaning is much the same. Reviewers should check the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting. Literal keeps the article.

decisions.choice: parceled out (B); cut up, with a piece for each group (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable bring out the picture of sharing out portions (m2).

source.text: μὴ Παῦλος ἐσταυρώθη ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν, ἢ εἰς τὸ ὄνομα Παύλου ἐβαπτίσθητε;

records.literal_gloss: Not Paul was crucified for you, or into the name of Paul were you baptized?

en.L: Paul was not crucified for you, was he? Or were you baptized into the name of Paul?
en.B: Was it Paul who was crucified for you? Or were you baptized into Paul's name?
en.R: Did Paul die on a cross for you? No! Were you baptized to belong to Paul? Of course not!

decisions.choice: questions expecting the answer "no"
decisions.reason: μὴ at the start marks a question that expects "no". The idea is absurd: Paul did not die for them, and they were not baptized to belong to him.

decisions.choice: crucified for you: a death on their behalf, which only Christ died
decisions.reason: ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ("for you") is the language of Christ's death for his people (15:3; 2 Corinthians 5:14-15). Only the one who died for them can claim them.

decisions.choice: baptized into the name: handed over to belong to someone
alternatives: baptized with a set form of words
decisions.reason: To be baptized "into the name" of someone meant to be made over to him as his own (compare Matthew 28:19). In Greek business usage, money paid "into the name" of someone was credited to his account. Believers are baptized into Christ, so they belong to him alone.

decisions.choice: Paul was not crucified for you, was he?
decisions.reason: Literal shows the question that expects "no" (m1) with a tag question.

decisions.choice: No! ... Of course not!
decisions.reason: Readable states the answer the questions expect (m1), so that young readers do not miss the point.

decisions.choice: die on a cross
decisions.reason: Readable says what crucifixion is.

source.text: εὐχαριστῶ ὅτι οὐδένα ὑμῶν ἐβάπτισα εἰ μὴ Κρίσπον καὶ Γάϊον, ἵνα μή τις εἴπῃ ὅτι εἰς τὸ ἐμὸν ὄνομα ἐβαπτίσθητε·

records.literal_gloss: I give thanks that none of you I baptized except Crispus and Gaius, \v 15 so that not anyone may say that into the my name you were baptized;

en.L: I give thanks that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, \v 15 so that no one may say that you were baptized into my name.
en.B: As things are, I am thankful that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, \v 15 so that no one can claim you were baptized into my name.
en.R: Now I am thankful that the only ones among you I baptized were Crispus and Gaius. \v 15 So no one can say that you were baptized to belong to me.

decisions.choice: Crispus and Gaius: two leading believers in Corinth
decisions.reason: Acts 18:8 says that Crispus, the leader of the synagogue in Corinth, believed with his whole household. Gaius was host to Paul and to the whole church when Paul wrote Romans from Corinth (Romans 16:23).

decisions.choice: so that: a result Paul sees looking back, not the reason he baptized few
alternatives: Paul baptized few people in order to prevent this
decisions.reason: ἵνα can express purpose or result. Paul could not have foreseen the slogans; he is glad now that, as things turned out, no one can use his baptism as a badge.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "I give thanks"
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts add "to God", as in verse 4; some important early manuscripts do not have it. A copyist was more likely to add the words than to drop them. The meaning is the same: Paul's thanks are to God.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "you were baptized"
decisions.reason: Later manuscripts read "that I baptized into my own name". The SBLGNT follows the early manuscripts. The meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: As things are (B); Now (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable show that Paul's thanks look back on what has happened since (m2).

decisions.choice: baptized to belong to me
decisions.reason: Readable says what being baptized into someone's name means (see the meaning decision on verse 13).

source.text: ἐβάπτισα δὲ καὶ τὸν Στεφανᾶ οἶκον· λοιπὸν οὐκ οἶδα εἴ τινα ἄλλον ἐβάπτισα.

records.literal_gloss: I baptized but also the of Stephanas household; beyond that I do not know if any other I baptized.

en.L: Now I also baptized the household of Stephanas; beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.
en.B: Yes, I also baptized the household of Stephanas. Beyond them, I am not aware that I baptized anyone else.
en.R: Oh yes, I also baptized Stephanas and the people of his household. I do not know of anyone else I baptized.

decisions.choice: household: the family and others who lived under one head, including slaves and dependents
decisions.reason: An οἶκον in the Roman world was the whole household under its head. Stephanas's household were the first believers in Achaia and served the church (16:15), and Stephanas was with Paul when he wrote (16:17), so he could remind Paul of this baptism.

decisions.choice: an afterthought: Paul corrects himself as he writes
decisions.reason: δὲ καὶ ("but also") adds a case Paul had left out, and λοιπὸν means "for the rest" or "beyond that". Paul did not keep count of whom he baptized, which itself shows that baptizing was not the center of his task (verse 17).

decisions.choice: Yes (B); Oh yes (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable show that Paul is correcting himself as he dictates (m2).

decisions.choice: Stephanas and the people of his household
decisions.reason: Readable says who belonged to a household (m1).

source.text: οὐ γὰρ ἀπέστειλέν με Χριστὸς βαπτίζειν ἀλλὰ εὐαγγελίζεσθαι, οὐκ ἐν σοφίᾳ λόγου, ἵνα μὴ κενωθῇ ὁ σταυρὸς τοῦ Χριστοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: Not for sent me Christ to baptize but to proclaim good news, not in wisdom of word, so that not may be emptied the cross of the Christ.

en.L: For {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel, not in wisdom of speech, so that the cross of the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} would not be emptied.
en.B: For {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} did not send me to baptize; {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} sent me to preach the gospel, and not with polished, wise-sounding words, so that the cross of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} would not be robbed of its force.
en.R: {{christos:Christ|The Messiah}} did not send me to baptize people. He sent me to tell the good news. And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did not send me to tell it with clever words that sound wise. Clever words would take away the power of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}'s death on the cross.

decisions.choice: not to baptize but to preach: a contrast of priority, not a dismissal of baptism
decisions.reason: Paul did baptize (verses 14-16), and he speaks of baptism with weight elsewhere (12:13; Romans 6:3-4). The "not ... but" sets out what his commission was for: εὐαγγελίζεσθαι, to announce the good news. As one "sent" (ἀπέστειλέν), he is an apostle (verse 1).

decisions.choice: wisdom of word: the art of persuasive, polished speaking that wins admiration
decisions.reason: σοφίᾳ λόγου is literally "wisdom of word". Greek cities, Corinth among them, admired trained public speakers and judged teachers by their eloquence. Paul refuses to rest the gospel on such skill (2:1-5). Verse 18 sets this against "the word of the cross".

decisions.choice: emptied: drained of its force and meaning
decisions.reason: κενωθῇ means to empty or make void. If the message won people by the speaker's brilliance, their faith would rest on him and not on the cross (2:5), and the cross would lose its power to save.

decisions.choice: the cross: Christ's death by crucifixion, the center of the message
decisions.reason: Crucifixion was the Roman punishment for slaves and rebels, the most shameful of deaths. That this is the heart of Paul's message is what makes it seem foolish (verses 18 and 23).

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting. Literal keeps the article at the end of the verse: "the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}".

decisions.choice: polished, wise-sounding words (B); clever words that sound wise (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "wisdom of word" means (m2) and keep the word "wise", which runs through verses 17-31.

decisions.choice: Clever words would take away the power of Christ's death on the cross
alternatives: so that the cross of Christ would not be emptied
decisions.reason: Readable says what "the cross" stands for and what "emptied" means (m3, m4).

source.text: Ὁ λόγος γὰρ ὁ τοῦ σταυροῦ τοῖς μὲν ἀπολλυμένοις μωρία ἐστίν, τοῖς δὲ σῳζομένοις ἡμῖν δύναμις θεοῦ ἐστιν.

records.literal_gloss: The word for the [one] of the cross to the [ones] on one hand perishing foolishness is, to the [ones] but being saved, to us, power of God it is.

en.L: For the word of the cross, to those who are perishing, is foolishness, but to us who are being saved it is [the] power of God.
en.B: To those on the way to destruction, the message of the cross is foolishness; but to us who are being saved, it is God's power.
en.R: To people who are headed for destruction, the message about {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}'s death on the cross sounds foolish. But we are being saved, and to us this message is the power of God.

decisions.choice: the word of the cross: the message whose subject is Christ crucified
alternatives: reasoning or argument about the cross
decisions.reason: λόγος picks up "word" in verse 17: not polished speech, but a message about the cross. The repeated article stresses it: the message, the one about the cross.

decisions.choice: perishing and being saved: two groups on two paths, each still under way and completed at the end
decisions.reason: Both participles, ἀπολλυμένοις and σῳζομένοις, are present: a process now going on. Paul uses the same pair in 2 Corinthians 2:15. For him salvation is begun now and completed on the day of the Lord (verse 8; 3:15; 5:5).

decisions.choice: foolishness: something absurd, which sensible people laugh at
decisions.reason: μωρία is the first of a chain of words for foolishness in verses 18-28, set against a chain of words for wisdom. Paul turns the two around: what the world calls foolish is God's wisdom.

decisions.choice: the power of God: God's own power at work to save
decisions.reason: The message does not only describe God's power; it is the means by which God saves those who believe (verse 21; Romans 1:16). Paul might have been expected to call it "wisdom" against "foolishness"; he calls it power.

decisions.choice: on the way to destruction (B); headed for destruction (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable bring out the present tense (m2): these people are on a path that ends in ruin.

decisions.choice: foolishness
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep the same word for each use of this word family in verses 18-28, so that the reader can follow Paul's play on wisdom and foolishness (m3).

decisions.choice: Christ's death on the cross
decisions.reason: Readable says what "the cross" stands for, as in verse 17. {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} is supplied.

source.text: γέγραπται γάρ· Ἀπολῶ τὴν σοφίαν τῶν σοφῶν, καὶ τὴν σύνεσιν τῶν συνετῶν ἀθετήσω.

records.literal_gloss: It has been written for, I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of the understanding [ones] I will set aside.

en.L: For it is written, "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of the intelligent I will set aside."
en.B: For Scripture says, "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the cleverness of the clever I will bring to nothing."
en.R: In Scripture God says, "I will destroy the wisdom of wise people. I will throw out the cleverness of clever people."

decisions.choice: a quotation of Isaiah 29:14
decisions.reason: In Isaiah 29:13-14 God speaks against leaders in Jerusalem who honored him with their lips while their hearts were far from him, and who trusted their own plans (compare Isaiah 30:1-2). God says he will act in a way that will make their wisdom fail. Paul sees the same thing happening in the cross: God sets aside human wisdom.

decisions.choice: Paul's words follow the Greek Old Testament, which makes God the one who acts
decisions.reason: In the Hebrew of Isaiah 29:14 the wisdom of the wise "will perish" and the understanding of the discerning "will hide itself"; the Greek Old Testament turns both into actions of God: "I will destroy ... I will hide". Paul's words match the Greek except for the last verb, where he has "I will set aside", perhaps recalling Psalm 33:10, where the Lord sets aside the plans of the nations. Reviewers should check the wording of the Greek Old Testament.

decisions.choice: set aside: declare void, make count for nothing
decisions.reason: ἀθετήσω means to set aside as invalid, as one sets aside an agreement (Galatians 3:15). God does not argue with human cleverness; he cancels it.

decisions.choice: it is written: it stands written, with lasting authority
decisions.reason: γέγραπται is a perfect: what Scripture says stands and still speaks. Paul uses the same word to introduce the quotation in verse 31.

decisions.choice: Scripture says
decisions.reason: Balanced names the Scriptures, which "it is written" refers to; Literal keeps the Greek form.

decisions.choice: In Scripture God says
decisions.reason: In Isaiah 29:13-14 the speaker is God (m1); Readable names him so that young readers know who "I" is.

decisions.choice: the cleverness of the clever (B); the cleverness of clever people (R)
decisions.reason: The two Greek words are related, like "wisdom" and "wise" in the first line; Balanced and Readable keep the pair.

source.text: ποῦ σοφός;

records.literal_gloss: Where wise [one]?

en.L: Where [is the] wise [one]?
en.B: Where is the wise person?
en.R: So where are the wise people?

decisions.choice: an echo of Isaiah's mocking questions: the wise are nowhere to be found
decisions.reason: Isaiah 19:11-12 asks of Pharaoh's advisers, "Where are your wise men now?", and Isaiah 33:18 asks "Where is the scribe?" of the oppressors who have vanished. Paul's three questions take up these words: when God acts, the wise of the world have nothing to say.

decisions.choice: the wise: the learned and the thinkers of any people, Greek or Jewish
decisions.reason: σοφός is general. The next two questions name a Jewish expert and a Greek-style debater, so this first one may cover both.

decisions.choice: So where are the wise people?
decisions.reason: Readable adds "So" to show that the questions follow from the quotation, and makes the question plural.

source.text: ποῦ γραμματεύς;

records.literal_gloss: Where scribe?

en.L: Where [is the] scribe?
en.B: Where is the expert in the Law?
en.R: Where are the teachers of the Law?

decisions.choice: scribe: a Jewish expert in the Law of Moses
decisions.reason: γραμματεύς could mean a public official, but in the Gospels it names teachers of the Law, and Isaiah 33:18 stands behind the question (see the decision on the first question of this verse). Paired with "the wise" and "the debater", it stands for Jewish learning.

decisions.choice: expert in the Law (B); teachers of the Law (R)
decisions.reason: Today "scribe" suggests someone who copies texts; Balanced and Readable say what the word meant.

source.text: ποῦ συζητητὴς τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου;

records.literal_gloss: Where debater of the age this?

en.L: Where [is the] debater of this age?
en.B: Where is the skilled debater of this present age?
en.R: Where are the great debaters of this present age?

decisions.choice: debater: one skilled in argument, as taught in the schools of philosophy and rhetoric
decisions.reason: συζητητὴς is a rare word for someone who disputes and debates. Greek cities prized such skill, and Jewish teachers also debated the Law; the word may cover both.

decisions.choice: this age: the present order of things, which is passing away before the age to come
decisions.reason: Jewish teaching set "this age" against "the age to come". Paul uses the phrase for a world whose wisdom and rulers are coming to nothing (2:6, 2:8; 3:18; 7:31). It may belong to all three questions, not only the last.

decisions.choice: skilled debater (B); great debaters (R); this present age (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what kind of person a debater was (m1), and "present" shows that "this age" is a span of time that will end (m2).

source.text: οὐχὶ ἐμώρανεν ὁ θεὸς τὴν σοφίαν τοῦ κόσμου;

records.literal_gloss: Not made foolish the God the wisdom of the world?

en.L: Did God not make foolish the wisdom of the world?
en.B: Has God not shown the world's wisdom to be foolishness?
en.R: God has shown that the wisdom of the world is foolish.

decisions.choice: a question expecting the answer "yes"
decisions.reason: οὐχὶ marks a question that expects agreement: yes, God has done this.

decisions.choice: made foolish: exposed as foolish, shown to be folly by what God has done in the cross
decisions.reason: ἐμώρανεν means to make foolish. God has not argued the world's wisdom down; by saving people through a crucified Messiah he has shown that it could not find him (verse 21; compare Isaiah 44:25).

decisions.choice: the world: human society and its ways of thinking, apart from God
decisions.reason: κόσμου here means humankind as it thinks and lives without God, as in verses 21 and 27-28.

decisions.choice: God has shown that ...
decisions.reason: The question expects "yes" (m1); Readable gives the answer as a plain statement.

decisions.choice: shown ... to be foolishness
decisions.reason: Balanced says how God made it foolish (m2) and keeps the word "foolishness" (see verse 18).

source.text: ἐπειδὴ γὰρ ἐν τῇ σοφίᾳ τοῦ θεοῦ οὐκ ἔγνω ὁ κόσμος διὰ τῆς σοφίας τὸν θεόν, εὐδόκησεν ὁ θεὸς διὰ τῆς μωρίας τοῦ κηρύγματος σῶσαι τοὺς πιστεύοντας.

records.literal_gloss: Since for in the wisdom of the God not knew the world through the wisdom the God, was pleased the God through the foolishness of the preaching to save the [ones] believing.

en.L: For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through [its] wisdom, God was pleased through the foolishness of the preaching to save those who believe.
en.B: For in God's wisdom the world, with all its wisdom, did not come to know {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. So it was God's good pleasure to save those who believe through the message we preach, foolishness though it seems.
en.R: God in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} wisdom made sure that the world would not come to know {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} by its own wisdom. Instead, God decided to save those who believe through the message we preach, a message that sounds foolish.

decisions.choice: in the wisdom of God: by God's wise purpose it came about that the world did not know him through its own wisdom
alternatives: though surrounded by the signs of God's wisdom in creation, the world failed to know him (compare Romans 1:19-21)
decisions.reason: σοφίᾳ τοῦ θεοῦ may describe God's wise plan, which allowed human wisdom to fail so that salvation would come as a gift; or the wisdom God showed in creation, which the world saw and still did not know him. The first fits Paul's point here, that God has made the world's wisdom foolish (verse 20); the second fits Romans 1. Both say that human wisdom could not reach God.

decisions.choice: through its wisdom: human wisdom, as a way to God, failed
decisions.reason: The article in τῆς σοφίας points to the world's own wisdom, just mentioned in verse 20. The world did not lack cleverness, but cleverness did not lead it to know God.

decisions.choice: the preaching: the message proclaimed, Christ crucified, not the act or style of preaching
alternatives: the foolish act of preaching itself
decisions.reason: κηρύγματος names what a herald announces. What seems foolish is the content, a crucified Messiah (verse 23), not the speaking.

decisions.choice: was pleased: chose freely, as his good purpose
decisions.reason: εὐδόκησεν is used of God's free decision (Galatians 1:15; Colossians 1:19). Saving people through this message was God's chosen way, not an accident.

decisions.choice: the message we preach, foolishness though it seems (B); a message that sounds foolish (R)
decisions.reason: Paul calls the message "foolishness" with irony: it is what the world counts foolish (verses 18 and 25). Balanced and Readable make the irony clear; Literal keeps his phrase.

decisions.choice: God in his wisdom made sure that
decisions.reason: Readable states the sense chosen in m1.

source.text: ἐπειδὴ καὶ Ἰουδαῖοι σημεῖα αἰτοῦσιν καὶ Ἕλληνες σοφίαν ζητοῦσιν·

records.literal_gloss: Since both Jews signs ask and Greeks wisdom seek;

en.L: For Jews ask for signs, and Greeks seek wisdom.
en.B: Jews ask for signs, and Greeks look for wisdom.
en.R: Jewish people ask for signs, acts of power that prove God is at work. Greeks want wisdom that makes sense to them.

decisions.choice: since indeed: a further reason, which leads into verse 23 ("but we preach")
alternatives: a clause that depends on verse 23: "Since Jews ask ..., we preach"
decisions.reason: ἐπειδὴ καὶ ("since also") picks up the reasoning of verse 21. The SBLGNT ends the verse with a raised dot, so the clause stands on its own and every level renders it as a statement; verse 23 then answers it with "but we".

decisions.choice: signs: acts of power that would prove God was behind a message
decisions.reason: Jews looked for God to act with power, as he had at the Exodus, and asked Jesus for σημεῖα (Mark 8:11; John 6:30). A Messiah who died in weakness gave them none.

decisions.choice: Greeks: people of Greek language and culture, standing here for non-Jews in general
decisions.reason: Ἕλληνες were known for philosophy and the love of argument. In verse 23 Paul uses the word "Gentiles" for the same group, and in verse 24 "Greeks" again.

decisions.choice: signs, acts of power that prove God is at work; wisdom that makes sense to them
decisions.reason: Readable says what kind of sign and what kind of wisdom each group wanted (m2, m3).

source.text: ἡμεῖς δὲ κηρύσσομεν Χριστὸν ἐσταυρωμένον, Ἰουδαίοις μὲν σκάνδαλον ἔθνεσιν δὲ μωρίαν, αὐτοῖς δὲ τοῖς κλητοῖς, Ἰουδαίοις τε καὶ Ἕλλησιν, Χριστὸν θεοῦ δύναμιν καὶ θεοῦ σοφίαν.

records.literal_gloss: We but preach Christ having been crucified, to Jews on one hand stumbling block, to Gentiles but foolishness, \v 24 to them but the called [ones], Jews both and Greeks, Christ of God power and of God wisdom.

en.L: But we preach {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} crucified, to Jews a stumbling block and to Gentiles foolishness, \v 24 but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} [the] power of God and [the] wisdom of God.
en.B: But we proclaim {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} crucified. To Jews this is an offense they stumble over, and to Gentiles it is foolishness, \v 24 but to those whom God has called, Jews and Greeks alike, {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} is God's power and God's wisdom.
en.R: But we tell people about {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, who died on a cross. Jewish people are offended by this message, and other people think it is foolish. \v 24 But God has called some people, both Jews and Greeks. To them {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

decisions.choice: Christ crucified: the Messiah who was crucified, and who remains the crucified one
decisions.reason: ἐσταυρωμένον is a perfect participle: the crucified one is what he is, even as the risen Lord (2:2; Galatians 3:1). To Jews a crucified Messiah was a contradiction: the Messiah was to triumph, and the Law says that anyone hanged on a tree is under God's curse (Deuteronomy 21:22-23; Galatians 3:13).

decisions.choice: stumbling block: something that trips people up and gives deep offense
decisions.reason: σκάνδαλον is the trigger of a trap, then anything that makes someone fall. Paul uses it of Christ in Romans 9:33, echoing Isaiah 8:14. Jews looking for signs of power tripped over a Messiah who died in weakness.

decisions.choice: the called: those God has called, who see in the same crucified Christ God's power and wisdom
decisions.reason: κλητοῖς picks up the call of verses 1, 2, 9 and 26: God's call that brings people to faith. The second Χριστὸν repeats the object of "we preach": the same message that offends others is, to the called, God's power and wisdom.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "to Gentiles"
decisions.reason: Later manuscripts read "to Greeks", matching verses 22 and 24; the early manuscripts have "Gentiles". The meaning is the same. Reviewers should check the apparatus.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting. The title setting matters here: a crucified Messiah was the offense (m1).

decisions.choice: an offense they stumble over (B); are offended (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps both the picture and the sense (m2); Readable gives the sense.

decisions.choice: other people
decisions.reason: "Gentiles" is church language for non-Jews; Readable uses plain words.

source.text: ὅτι τὸ μωρὸν τοῦ θεοῦ σοφώτερον τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐστίν, καὶ τὸ ἀσθενὲς τοῦ θεοῦ ἰσχυρότερον τῶν ἀνθρώπων.

records.literal_gloss: Because the foolish [thing] of the God wiser than the humans is, and the weak [thing] of the God stronger than the humans.

en.L: Because the foolish [thing] of God is wiser than humans, and the weak [thing] of God [is] stronger than humans.
en.B: For the foolish thing God has done is wiser than any human wisdom, and the weak thing God has done is stronger than any human strength.
en.R: What looks like foolishness from God is wiser than all human wisdom. What looks like weakness from God is stronger than all human strength.

decisions.choice: the foolish thing of God: what God has done that seems foolish and weak, the cross
alternatives: foolishness and weakness as qualities in God
decisions.reason: μωρὸν and ἀσθενὲς are neuter adjectives with the article: "the foolish thing", "the weak thing". Paul is not saying God is foolish or weak, but that what God has done in a crucified Messiah, which looks foolish and weak, outdoes everything human beings can do (2 Corinthians 13:4).

decisions.choice: wiser than humans: wiser than humans are, wiser than all their wisdom
decisions.reason: The comparison is short: σοφώτερον τῶν ἀνθρώπων is "wiser than humans", meaning wiser than human wisdom; likewise with strength. The shorthand makes the point bluntly.

decisions.choice: the foolish thing God has done; any human wisdom (B); what looks like foolishness from God; all human wisdom (R)
alternatives: the foolishness of God is wiser than men
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable spell out what "the foolish thing of God" refers to (m1) and complete the comparison (m2). Literal keeps "humans", which is already inclusive.

source.text: Βλέπετε γὰρ τὴν κλῆσιν ὑμῶν, ἀδελφοί, ὅτι οὐ πολλοὶ σοφοὶ κατὰ σάρκα, οὐ πολλοὶ δυνατοί, οὐ πολλοὶ εὐγενεῖς·

records.literal_gloss: Look at for the calling of you, brothers, that not many wise according to flesh, not many powerful, not many well-born;

en.L: For consider your calling, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}: not many [were] wise according to [the] flesh, not many powerful, not many well-born.
en.B: Just look at your own calling, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}. When God called you, not many of you were wise as people measure wisdom, not many held power, not many came from leading families.
en.R: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, think about who you were when God called you. Not many of you were wise in the eyes of other people. Not many of you were important or powerful. Not many came from important families.

decisions.choice: look at: an appeal to consider what they can see for themselves
decisions.reason: Βλέπετε can be a command ("look at") or a statement ("you see"). Either way Paul points to the church itself as proof of what he has said.

decisions.choice: your calling: God's call that brought you to faith, and the kind of people you were when it came
alternatives: your job or position in life
decisions.reason: κλῆσιν is God's act of calling (verses 2, 9, 24). Here Paul asks them to think of who they were when the call came. In 7:20 the word comes close to meaning one's position in life.

decisions.choice: according to the flesh: by human standards
decisions.reason: κατὰ σάρκα means judged as people judge, apart from God, as in Philippians 3:3-4. The phrase may belong to all three lines.

decisions.choice: powerful and well-born: people of influence and of noble family
decisions.reason: Corinth was a Roman colony where rank, wealth and family mattered greatly. δυνατοί are people of power and influence; εὐγενεῖς are people of good birth. "Not many" means that a few were: Crispus, Gaius, and Erastus the city treasurer (Romans 16:23).

decisions.choice: {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}
decisions.reason: As in verse 10.

decisions.choice: as people measure wisdom (B); in the eyes of other people (R)
decisions.reason: In everyday English "flesh" means the body; Balanced and Readable give the sense (m3).

decisions.choice: When God called you (B); who you were when God called you (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "your calling" refers to here (m2).

source.text: ἀλλὰ τὰ μωρὰ τοῦ κόσμου ἐξελέξατο ὁ θεός, ἵνα καταισχύνῃ τοὺς σοφούς, καὶ τὰ ἀσθενῆ τοῦ κόσμου ἐξελέξατο ὁ θεός, ἵνα καταισχύνῃ τὰ ἰσχυρά, καὶ τὰ ἀγενῆ τοῦ κόσμου καὶ τὰ ἐξουθενημένα ἐξελέξατο ὁ θεός, τὰ μὴ ὄντα, ἵνα τὰ ὄντα καταργήσῃ, ὅπως μὴ καυχήσηται πᾶσα σὰρξ ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: But the foolish [things] of the world chose the God, so that he might shame the wise, and the weak [things] of the world chose the God, so that he might shame the strong [things], \v 28 and the low-born [things] of the world and the despised [things] chose the God, the [things] not being, so that the [things] being he might bring to nothing, \v 29 so that not may boast all flesh before the God.

en.L: But God chose the foolish things of the world so that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} might put the wise to shame, and God chose the weak things of the world so that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} might put the strong things to shame, \v 28 and God chose the low-born things of the world and the despised things, the things that are not, so that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} might bring to nothing the things that are, \v 29 so that no flesh might boast before God.
en.B: Instead, God chose what the world counts foolish, to put the wise to shame. God chose what the world counts weak, to put the strong to shame. \v 28 God chose what the world counts low and despises, things that are nothing, to cancel out the things that are something, \v 29 so that no human being could ever boast in God's presence.
en.R: But God chose people the world thinks are foolish, to make wise people ashamed. God chose people the world thinks are weak, to make the strong ashamed. \v 28 God chose people the world looks down on and thinks are not important, people who seem to be nothing. He did this to bring to nothing the people who seem to be something. \v 29 So no one can ever boast in front of God.

decisions.choice: the foolish things, the weak things: people, spoken of as things, the Corinthians themselves among them
decisions.reason: The forms are neuter plural (μωρὰ, ἀσθενῆ), but after verse 26 Paul means people: those the world thinks little of. The neuter makes the description general and blunt. Against them stand "the wise" (σοφούς, masculine) and "the strong things".

decisions.choice: of the world: foolish, weak and low in the world's eyes
alternatives: the foolish people who are part of the world
decisions.reason: The genitive τοῦ κόσμου can mean "belonging to the world" or "as the world sees it". The contrast with God's choice favors the second: they are foolish by the world's measure, not by God's.

decisions.choice: the things that are not: people who count for nothing; to bring to nothing: to cancel the power of those who count for something
alternatives: things that do not exist at all
decisions.reason: μὴ ὄντα ("not being") means those who are nobodies in the world's eyes. καταργήσῃ means to make powerless or put out of action (2:6; 15:24). The words may recall God who calls into being things that are not (Romans 4:17): God's choice makes something of nobodies.

decisions.choice: all flesh: every human being
decisions.reason: πᾶσα σὰρξ is an Old Testament way of saying "every person", stressing human weakness before God (Isaiah 40:5-6). No one can claim credit before God; Jeremiah's words in verse 31 say the same.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "the things that are not" without "and"
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts read "and" before "the things that are not", making it one more item in the list. The SBLGNT follows important early manuscripts without it, so the phrase sums up the list: the low and despised are "things that are not". Reviewers should check the apparatus.

decisions.choice: what the world counts foolish ... weak ... low
alternatives: the foolish things of the world
decisions.reason: Balanced states the sense chosen in m2.

decisions.choice: people the world thinks are foolish ... weak ... looks down on
alternatives: the foolish things of the world
decisions.reason: Readable says that Paul is speaking of people (m1).

decisions.choice: no human being (B); no one (R)
decisions.reason: The idiom means every person (m4); Literal keeps "flesh".

decisions.choice: He did this to bring to nothing ...
alternatives: to bring to nothing the things that are
decisions.reason: Readable breaks the long sentence and makes God the subject of a new one.

source.text: ἐξ αὐτοῦ δὲ ὑμεῖς ἐστε ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, ὃς ἐγενήθη σοφία ἡμῖν ἀπὸ θεοῦ, δικαιοσύνη τε καὶ ἁγιασμὸς καὶ ἀπολύτρωσις, ἵνα καθὼς γέγραπται· Ὁ καυχώμενος ἐν κυρίῳ καυχάσθω.

records.literal_gloss: From him but you are in Christ Jesus, who became wisdom for us from God, righteousness both and holiness and redemption, \v 31 so that just as it has been written, The [one] boasting in [the] Lord let him boast.

en.L: But from {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} you are in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus, who became wisdom for us from God, both righteousness and holiness and redemption, \v 31 so that, just as it is written, "The one who boasts must boast in [the] Lord."
en.B: It is God who has placed you in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has become God's wisdom for us, which means our righteousness, our holiness and our redemption. \v 31 So, as Scripture says, "Whoever boasts should boast in the Lord."
en.R: God is the one who has joined you to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus. {{christos:Christ|The Messiah}} is God's wisdom for us. Because of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} we are righteous in God's sight, we are made holy, and we are set free. \v 31 So, as Scripture says, "Anyone who wants to boast should boast only about the Lord."

decisions.choice: from him: God is the source; their being in Christ is his doing
decisions.reason: αὐτοῦ refers back to God, named at the end of verse 29. Their new life "in Christ Jesus" comes from God, not from their own wisdom or rank, so there is nothing to boast of.

decisions.choice: righteousness, holiness and redemption spell out what "wisdom from God" is
alternatives: four separate gifts: wisdom, righteousness, holiness and redemption
decisions.reason: τε καὶ ("both ... and") ties the last three words closely together and sets them a little apart from σοφία. The point of the passage is wisdom, so the three most likely explain what God's wisdom in Christ is: not clever ideas, but what Christ has done for us. Read as four gifts, the sense is close.

decisions.choice: righteousness: being in the right with God, given in Christ
decisions.reason: δικαιοσύνη here is what Christ is "for us": the right standing with God that God gives (2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9).

decisions.choice: holiness: being set apart for God, made his own
alternatives: a gradual process of moral improvement only
decisions.reason: ἁγιασμὸς belongs with "made holy" and "holy ones" in verse 2: in Christ they belong to God.

decisions.choice: redemption: release, as of a slave set free
alternatives: the payment of a price, as the main idea
decisions.reason: ἀπολύτρωσις means setting free, as a slave or captive was set free (Colossians 1:14). Paul will remind the Corinthians that they were bought with a price (6:20; 7:23).

decisions.choice: a shortened quotation of Jeremiah 9:23-24 (9:22-23 in the Hebrew numbering)
decisions.reason: Jeremiah 9:23-24 says: let not the wise boast of wisdom, nor the mighty of might, nor the rich of riches, but let the one who boasts boast of this, that he understands and knows God. These are the very people of verse 26: the wise, the powerful and the well-born. Paul sums up the passage in one line; the Greek of 1 Samuel 2:10 has similar words. He uses the same line in 2 Corinthians 10:17.

decisions.choice: the Lord: in Jeremiah, God's own name; here most likely Christ Jesus
decisions.reason: In the Hebrew of Jeremiah 9:24 the word is the divine name, YHWH. Paul quotes it with κυρίῳ ("Lord"), and after verse 30, where everything comes to believers "in Christ Jesus", the Lord in whom they boast is most likely Christ. As with "calling on the name of the Lord" (verse 2), a text about God himself is applied to Jesus.

decisions.choice: so that: Paul leaves the verb unspoken, "so that it may be as it is written"
decisions.reason: ἵνα is followed directly by the quotation, with no verb of its own. The sense is clear: God has acted in this way so that the Scripture may hold true.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting. Readable supplies the title again where it begins a new sentence.

decisions.choice: Lord
decisions.reason: The style guide keeps "the LORD" for the divine name in the Old Testament itself. Here Paul quotes the verse with the Greek word for "Lord", as John 1:23 does; meaning decision m7 explains whom it means.

decisions.choice: It is God who has placed you in (B); God is the one who has joined you to (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name God as the source (m1).

decisions.choice: we are righteous in God's sight
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the key term as "righteous" and says what it means here (m3).

decisions.choice: The one who boasts must boast (L); Whoever boasts should boast (B); Anyone who wants to boast should boast only (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek is a command in the third person. English has no exact match, so each level uses "must" or "should" and avoids a masculine pronoun for a saying that applies to anyone.
